canberra.title: Greens walk away from Labor deal but rule out move to topple government
canberra.snippet: The ACT Greens have ruled out a new confidence and supply agreement with Labor for the remainder of the term after the two parties failed...
canberra.content:
ACT Greens leader Jo Clay said the Greens aren’t planning to bring down the Labor Government, or make a deal with the Canberra Liberals. Photo: Ian Bushnell.

The ACT Greens have ruled out a new confidence and supply agreement with Labor for the remainder of the term after the two parties failed to agree on firm commitments covering renters, libraries, disability support, climate and the environment.

But Greens Leader Jo Clay stressed the decision would not trigger an election, and her party was not seeking to bring down the Labor Government or form an alternative government with the Canberra Liberals.

Instead, the Greens will remain on the crossbench, leaving the minority government to secure the numbers it needs in the Legislative Assembly as individual matters arise.

Ms Clay said the sticking point was not necessarily the policies themselves, but Labor’s unwillingness to commit to what would be delivered and by when.

“So it was that lack of accountability that is what fell through,” Ms Clay said.

Labor rejected that characterisation, saying there was substantial common ground but it could not agree to some fixed delivery dates, specific funding commitments and prescribed ways of implementing policy.

The decision ends negotiations that began in August and leaves the parties to work together issue by issue and budget by budget for the rest of the term.

Chief Minister Andrew Barr said there were also some proposals Labor simply could not support.

“We approached these discussions constructively and in good faith. While we were unable to reach agreement on every issue, they were positive and productive conversations that identified substantial areas of common ground,” Mr Barr said.

“It’s disappointing we could not find compromise on some issues in the best interest of delivering a shared progressive policy agenda for Canberra.”

Andrew Barr was disappointed that agreement would not be reached to deliver a “progressive policy agenda”. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

The Greens say that over several rounds of negotiations, Labor would not commit within this term to a portable rental bond scheme and a stronger Rental Ombudsman, or to restoring weekend services at Kippax and Erindale libraries by July 2027.

They also sought protection for the Western Edge and conservation areas, greater shared decision-making with Traditional Custodians, stronger gambling harm reduction measures and an end to government funding for horse racing.

On climate, the Greens wanted at least $5 million a year to implement the government’s climate action plan and a clear plan to phase out petrol and diesel transport.

They also wanted Labor to spend $90 million already allocated by the ACT Government for foundational disability supports, to prevent what the Greens described as a potential “cliff edge” for Canberrans who will lose or have their NDIS supports reduced.

“These are reasonable things to request for the community. They are all consistent with what Canberrans have told us they want,” Ms Clay said.

Labor, however, said the disagreement in many cases was about how policies should be implemented rather than the objective itself.

The government said it was willing to support the broad intent of several proposals but could not accept highly prescriptive implementation pathways, fixed deadlines, specified funding commitments or predetermined policy mechanisms.

It said decisions needed to remain informed by consultation, budget processes, implementation and operational considerations, emerging evidence and the Territory’s financial circumstances.

One point of contention Ms Clay highlighted was Canberra’s libraries.

The Greens wanted weekend services at Kippax and Erindale restored by July 2027, pointing to more than 3500 Canberrans who have called for weekend access.

Ms Clay also criticised Labor’s position on horse racing, saying that while the government would not accept the Greens’ demands, it had sought their support for another six years of funding for the racing industry.

Mr Barr rejected the broader suggestion that the failure to reach a deal reflected a lack of willingness by Labor to act.

“The suggestion that this outcome reflects a lack of ambition or commitment from the government is simply wrong,” he said.

“Labor is getting on with the job of building more homes, strengthening public services, supporting jobs and economic growth, advancing climate action and delivering on our commitments to Canberrans.”

The Greens’ insistence on deadlines was partly driven by their experience with the previous confidence-and-supply agreement.

After the 2024 election, former Greens leader Shane Rattenbury reached an agreement with Mr Barr that saw the Greens move to the crossbench and support him as Chief Minister in exchange for a series of policy commitments. That agreement expired when Mr Rattenbury retired.

Ms Clay said the Greens believed commitments from that agreement involving household food organics and garden organics (FOGO), protection of the Ainslie Volcanics and maternity services had either been breached or were unlikely to be delivered.

Despite walking away from a new deal, the Greens will support passage of the current ACT Budget.

Ms Clay said earlier Budget negotiations had resulted in concessions including preventing the return of the health levy and increasing funding for the community sector.

“This budget is not perfect, but this budget is a budget that the Greens will support passage of, but we will need to discuss future budgets with the Labor government,” she said.

Ms Clay also ruled out another attempt to negotiate a confidence and supply agreement later this term. She said the Greens were not looking to form government with the Canberra Liberals.

Instead, Labor and Greens parliamentary leaders have agreed to meet before each sitting week, while the parties will also engage ahead of future budgets.

Labor said it would work with the Greens, independents and Liberals on a case-by-case basis to get legislation through the Assembly.

canberra.title: Brave mum fights off sex offender in terrifying underground ambush
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to sexual assault. A predator followed a woman into a deserted underground carpark before trying to ...
canberra.content:
The woman was staying at a hotel on Northbourne Avenue when Lai Ro Puia attacked her. Photo: James Coleman.

CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to sexual assault.

A predator followed a woman into a deserted underground carpark before trying to sexually assault her in a terrifying and violent attack.

The woman had booked a room at a hotel on Northbourne Avenue in November 2025 because she was visiting Canberra to collect her university student son, ACT Supreme Court Justice Andrew Muller said in his recently published decision.

She didn’t notice Lal Ro Puia following her when she drove into the hotel’s underground carpark that evening. After stopping her car, she opened her door to find him standing in front of her.

He asked her for money, food and a hug before grabbing her, pushing her to the ground and jumping on top of her. He tried to pull off her clothes while repeatedly shoving her head into the ground and dragging her across the ground.

The woman fought back, stabbing at his side with her car keys. Puia began taking off his own clothes before he got off her and left the scene.

The entire attack was caught on CCTV.

“One of its compelling features is the courageous attempts of [the woman] to resist and fight off her attacker where opportunity presented to do so,” Justice Muller said.

The woman told the court about her shock, fear and hopelessness as a consequence of the assault occurring when she had no defender and felt increasingly unable to resist her attacker.

“My hope is that no other person experiences such a predator, and that the public are assured of safety and support within the community,” she said.

Puia, who is originally from Myanmar, was 13 when he came to Australia with his family as refugees in 2008.

The now-31-year-old has been diagnosed with schizophrenia, polysubstance use and borderline personality traits.

Justice Muller said he had been living an increasingly itinerant and homeless lifestyle, but had been staying with his father in Queanbeyan before he was arrested in November 2025.

He said Puia had been on the disability support pension for about 10 years, presumably due to his mental health difficulties.

The judge noted the authors of a court report found there had been an increasing frequency of his sexual offending and a sporadic engagement with mental health services.

He has an extensive history of offending across the ACT, NSW and Victoria, including on charges of sexual assault and committing acts of indecency without consent.

Justice Muller said he would sentence Puia to a lengthy period of supervision in the community.

“I believe that offers the most likely path for Mr Puia to reach a point where he no longer presents as a threat to women,” he said.

Puia pleaded guilty to sexual assault in the second degree and burglary.

He was convicted and sentenced to five years’ jail with a two-year, nine-month non-parole period, backdated to account for time in custody. He will be eligible for release from August 2028.

If this story has raised any concerns for you, 1800RESPECT, the national 24-hour sexual assault, family and domestic violence counselling line, can be contacted on 1800 737 732. Help and support are also available through the Canberra Rape Crisis Centre on 6247 2525, the Domestic Violence Crisis Service ACT on 6280 0900, the Sexual Violence Legal Services on 6257 4377 and Lifeline on 13 11 14. In an emergency, call Triple Zero.

If you have been affected by sexual violence, or someone you know has, you can report it to authorities by attending a police station or phoning 131 444.

canberra.title: Minister says Comcare Scheme needs an overhaul to get injured APS workers back sooner
canberra.snippet: Labor is reforming the federal workers’ compensation scheme to streamline claims and get injured public servants back to work sooner. Emp...
canberra.content:
Employment Minister Amanda Rishworth says the Comcare Scheme for compensation is outdated. Photo: Comcare.

Labor is reforming the federal workers’ compensation scheme to streamline claims and get injured public servants back to work sooner.

Employment and Workplace Relations Minister Amanda Rishworth flagged the changes at the Comcare National Conference in Canberra on Wednesday (16 September), saying much of the Comcare Scheme was stuck in the 1980s when it was first legislated.

“I would like to recognise that in many respects, the Comcare scheme does provide quality support for injured workers, at a very difficult time for them,” the minister said.

“Of course, like with any public administration scheme, there have been significant changes to Comcare’s operating environment since 1988.

“But the scheme’s underpinning legislation and design have not kept pace with these changes.

“Comcare now covers a much wider range of work environments and types of work, compared to when it was first established.

“The nature of work has also changed, meaning the scheme must respond to a broader range of work-related hazards, injuries and rehabilitation needs.

“The jobs of today involve far more non-routine cognitive tasks and emotional demands, increasing the risk of exposure to psychosocial hazards.”

Ms Rishworth said the Comcare Scheme does not have enough emphasis on early intervention, as is the case with some state government schemes.

She outlined the principles for reforms she will be implementing to support what she said will be the scheme’s effective operation and future sustainability.

This includes creating a system with better early supports for injured workers, focusing on recovery and maintaining a close connection with work.

“Because there is clear evidence that early support is critical to the recovery and return to work for injured workers,” she said.

“And timely support also reduces the potential additional harms that can be caused by lengthy claims processes.”

The second principle is ensuring the rehabilitation and recovery process for workers is ultimately focused on supporting them to safely return to work.

The minister noted that the longer someone is out of the workplace because of injury, the less likely they are to return to work.

The third principle Ms Rishworth wants to embed in the government’s targeted reform process is modernising Comcare, particularly through its claims processes.

She wants claims management streamlined to be fast and efficient, so both workers and employers can focus on recovery and a safe return to work “rather than wrestling with paperwork”, and she wants the process to be more user-friendly.

The Federal Government is also looking at ways to improve the Comcare Scheme’s oversight and governance, with a view to ensuring it becomes fit-for-purpose into the future.

“For example, I am interested in how we can improve Comcare’s ability to engage with key stakeholders at a strategic level,” the minister said.

“This would help identify emerging trends and challenges, as well as improve the scheme’s ability to respond to a changing environment.

“I also believe there are opportunities to modernise the Comcare framework in a way that will improve communication, coordination and cooperation between all parties.

“Like making the allocation of return-to-work responsibilities between employers and rehabilitation authorities much clearer.

“This will help promote a person-centred approach that benefits both workers and employers.”

The planned changes come amid a backdrop of increased claims for psychological injuries in the Australian Public Service.

For APS agencies, return-to-work rates for psychological claims are 54 per cent, compared to 91 per cent for physical injury claims.

Comcare Deputy CEO Michael Duke provided data of the rise on psychological injury claims. Photo: Comcare.

Comcare deputy CEO Michael Duke told the conference that psychological claims now account for 47 per cent of open claims Comcare is managing, and for half of overall claims costs.

“Across Australian Government workers’ compensation claims, mental health conditions are now the most prevalent type of condition claimed,” he said.

“In the 2025-26 financial year alone, Comcare received 963 claims for psychological injury. This compares with 440 psychological claims received in 2021-22. That is more than double in number …

“As you would be aware, these claims experience longer periods of time off work and poorer return-to-work outcomes.

“Median incapacity or time off work is more than 32 weeks.”

canberra.title: Minister censured over cutting library hours despite Assembly’s directive to pause any action
canberra.snippet: Attorney-General Tara Cheyne has been censured by the Legislative Assembly for closing Canberra’s libraries on Sundays despite an A...
canberra.content:
Minister Tara Cheyne faced a censure motion over actions on Canberra’s library hours and legislation to fix an administrative error in issuing seatbelt infringements by mobile detection cameras. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

Attorney-General Tara Cheyne has been censured by the Legislative Assembly for closing Canberra’s libraries on Sundays despite an Assembly directive to hold off on the decision.

The Canberra Liberals’ original motion also sought to censure her over the administrative error that has called into question the legality of almost 13,000 fines issued by detection cameras for seatbelt offences.

“Ministers are meant to hold the public service to account. Instead we get libraries closed against the will of the Assembly, the wider Canberra community and thousands of drivers slugged with fines that should never have been issued,” Canberra Liberals leader Mark Parton said.

“Censure is the strongest tool this parliament has short of no confidence. If ministers can shrug off an Assembly motion and preside over unlawful infringements, responsible government is just a slogan.”

ACT Greens deputy leader Andrew Braddock narrowed the censure’s scope to just focus on the libraries.

A private members bill from 12 June included several requirements for the ACT Government, including not reducing library evening opening hours until pick-up lockers were available and pausing any proposed hours changes until the legislation enabling the budget passed.

But the ACT Government went ahead with changes on 27 August.

Mr Braddock took issue with this move, stating it went against community wishes.

“There’s an increasingly concerning pattern of Assembly resolutions being treated as optional rather than authoritative expressions of the will of the Parliament,” he said.

“When motions are passed by the Assembly, ministers have an obligation to take them seriously.”

Independent Kurrajong MLA Thomas Emerson attempted to have the censure motion downgraded to an admonishment.

He compared statements about Ms Cheyne’s actions to previous censure motions against Minister Chris Steel and now-backbencher Yvette Berry, saying the conduct wasn’t on the same level.

“I think, in this case, it’s not a matter of a minister’s incompetence; it’s not a matter of a lack of oversight – it’s a matter of us disagreeing with a decision that was made,” Mr Emerson said.

“We have other mechanisms to debate and condemn government decisions in the Assembly, while reserving censure motions for clear instances of government incompetence.

“I completely disagree with what the ACT Government’s doing to our libraries. But if we lower the threshold and start using censure motions for every disagreement, they risk becoming meaningless.”

Now-independent Yerrabi MLA Leanne Castley went further.

“We already know the Opposition clearly intends to censure, smear and whinge their way to the 2028 election,” she said of her former party.

“It’s not a winning strategy … it’s an electoral dead-end even at the best of times.”

The Canberra Liberals, ACT Greens and Murrumbidgee independent MLA Fiona Carrick voted down the attempt to downgrade the censure motion.

Ms Cheyne expressed astonishment that she could be censured for moving ahead with changes meant to fix underlying staffing and culture issues at Canberra’s libraries following a review.

“What most concerns me … is that I was clear during that debate on 12 June … about what I could and couldn’t do,” she said.

“I’m not sure how [much] clearer I could have been.”

During the 12 June debate (Hansard page 2427), she did state there would be difficulties in not changing evening opening hours (referred to as 5 (c)) and not making any changes before the budget legislation was debated (referred to as 5 (e)).

“I have to be clear; this is an operational reality. I cannot do 5(c), and I cannot do 5(e),” Ms Cheyne said at the time.

“I can try and do 5(c) as best as we possibly can – I will try – but I cannot do 5(e).”

Ms Cheyne added an amendment to the censure motion outlining the government’s commitment to expanding community access to ACT libraries, including prioritising weekend branch access at Kippax and Erindale from July 2027, and to publish an evaluation of the library operating arrangements by March 2027.

The Assembly standing orders state that if the government or a minister are unable to meet a deadline to undertake a certain action from an Assembly resolution, they “shall write to all Members of the Assembly directly informing them that the deadline will not be met and including the reasons for the delay”.

The Canberra Liberals, ACT Greens and independent Fiona Carrick voted to censure Ms Cheyne.

Deputy Chief Minister Rachel Stephen-Smith expressed her disbelief that her colleague had been censured “for not delivering the impossible”.

“It is extraordinary that this place is going to censure a minister for doing their job,” she said.

“I am very, very disappointed in [certain] members of this place.”

canberra.title: Defence personnel recruitment and retention numbers climb to 25-year high
canberra.snippet: The Australian Defence Force (ADF) has the largest number of permanent members in 25 years after a concerted recruitment and retention ef...
canberra.content:
In 2025/26, recruitment grew across all three ADF services. Photo: POIS Bradley Darvill.

The Australian Defence Force (ADF) has the largest number of permanent members in 25 years after a concerted recruitment and retention effort in recent years.

The Federal Government said the ADF had 8100 new enlistments in the 2025/26 financial year, the highest number since 2010, and said the full-time and permanent workforce now exceeded 64,000 personnel, the largest since 2001.

It said recruitment growth had improved across all three services, with the navy achieving its highest intake in 16 years, the army its highest in 12 years, and the air force its highest intake in 24 years.

These improved recruitment numbers have been further bolstered by a reduced separation rate, which dropped from 7.9 per cent to 7.4 per cent last year, the lowest since 2011.

More than $1 billion has been spent on recruitment and retention since 2022 after numbers stagnated in the decade before. For example, in 2021, the permanent ADF workforce shrank by 1400.

The previous high separation rate was linked to a boom in mining jobs, operational fatigue from continuous deployments to Iraq and Afghanistan, and weariness among ADF members who had repeatedly been called upon to support clean-ups after a series of natural disasters.

Adecco Australia took over Defence recruitment from Manpower in October 2022 on a reported $20 million-a-year contract.

In 2023, the former ‘’Defence Jobs’’ recruitment branding was changed to ‘’ADF Careers’’, which was relaunched under the command of a three-star officer and with four new fixed recruitment centres in Brisbane, Sydney, Melbourne and Perth, and one mobile run by Adecco.

The government offered a $400 million retention scheme to personnel who were nearing the end of their return of service obligation (ROSO) period. Under the scheme, defence members were offered a $50,000 bonus if they signed on for an additional three years after their initial ROSO period.

In 2023, an Australian National Audit Office report found that recruitment targets continued to fall short, with the ADF meeting only 73 per cent of its target in 2022-23. It also found Defence had no effective ways of measuring the success of its recruitment campaigns.

In early 2025, with recruitment numbers continuing to fall below the targeted rate, Defence Minister Richard Marles said the average processing time for an ADF applicant was 268 days, a figure he said was unacceptable and should be less than half that.

The statement came as it was reported the government was having “difficult conversations” with Adecco about the shortfall.

But the tide has seemingly turned, with the government claiming Defence received almost 74,000 applications in 2025-26, and that the ADF was back on track to achieve the government’s target of 69,000 permanent Average Funded Strength by the early 2030s.

In a 15 September statement, Mr Marles said more sailors, soldiers, aviators, and cyber and space operators joined the ADF than in the past 16 years.

“The men and women who wear our nation’s uniform go to work every day to keep Australians safe,” he said.

“That is why the government is focused on recruiting, retaining and skilling the workforce we need.

“We’ve already made significant progress, but we will continue to reform recruitment processes and retention initiatives over the long term.”

Minister for Defence Personnel Matt Keogh said Defence’s most important capability was its people.

“Thanks to the government’s interventions, the Defence workforce is growing, with more people putting their hand up to serve and more personnel choosing to stick around for longer,” he said.

“In 2026, a career in the ADF can mean almost anything, with more than 300 roles to choose from. It’s fantastic to see more Australians coming forward to serve in such dynamic and rewarding careers.”

At a media doorstop at Parliament House on Tuesday, Mr Marles said the government had completely turned things around.

“And we’ve done this by much better recruiting, by focusing on where people are at in terms of more emphasis online, less on TV,” he said.

“We’ve had really innovative recruitment practices such as pop-up recruiting centres, which have been very effective. We’re pulling people through the recruitment process much quicker; that’s been important.

“But we’re also paying people more across the Defence Force, particularly in those trades where we need more people.”

Original Article published by Andrew McLaughlin on PS News.

australia.title: ‘It’s how Jean does business’: fugitive developer left Jeremy Greenwood ‘high and dry’, Icac hears
australia.snippet: Greenwood denies that invoices for almost $1m sent in a single day in September 2021 were ‘bogus accounts’ to cover up political donation...
australia.content:
A Liberal factional figure has been left “high and dry” by fugitive property developer Jean Nassif, but did not chase him for payments because “it’s how Jean does business”, New South Wales’ anti-corruption watchdog has heard.

Jeremy Greenwood returned to the Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) on Wednesday after Nassif made an explosive video appearance from his Beirut bedroom on Monday and Tuesday. Nassif declared he was “not corrupt”.

Icac is investigating an allegation that Greenwood, Charles Perrottet and Christian Ellis shared in $2m in payments between 2020 and 2023 from Nassif, or his company Toplace, in exchange for political outcomes.

Greenwood and Perrottet have said payments were for genuine lobbying work by Beckington, controlled by Greenwood and Ellis, and JPG Advisory, controlled by Greenwood. Greenwood has previously described an agreement, which he said was written on a purple-pink piece of paper, under which they would be paid $1m for each Toplace development they could get fast-tracked.

On Wednesday afternoon, Greenwood denied that invoices purportedly “in arrears” of almost $1m sent in a single day by Beckington to Toplace in September 2021, were “bogus accounts to cover up the scheme where Nassif is paying large amounts of money [in political donations]”.

“There’s no scheme,” he said. Greenwood, who told the commission he did not believe Beckington received all the money owed to it by Toplace before it began to pay JPG Advisory in 2022, was asked why he had not followed this up with Nassif.

“You’ve met him now,” said Greenwood. “It’s how Jean does business.”

Greenwood has told the inquiry he is a creditor of Toplace, which collapsed in 2023 owing more than $1bn after Nassif fled for Lebanon in late 2022. On Wednesday, the commission heard that Christian Ellis was also a creditor and had publicly lodged that Beckington was owed $1.4m by Toplace for consultancy work between 2019 and 2021.

Greenwood, who has admitted to being in contact with Ellis during the inquiry, was asked if he had discussed with him “the proposition you were owed over $1m” by Nassif.

“I mean we’ve certainly discussed the fact that Jean, we believe, left us high and dry,” he said.

Counsel assisting, Peggy Dwyer SC put it to him that it “is not something that you would want to openly disclose, the consultancy work you did with Jean Nassif”. Greenwood said he had “no issue disclosing that I worked for Toplace”.

Questions over Anita Perrottet work

On Wednesday morning, Greenwood was asked about his previous evidence on advice he said Anita Perrottet, sister-in-law of the former premier, gave to lobbying firms Beckington, controlled by Greenwood and Ellis, and JPG Advisory, controlled by Greenwood.

Dwyer has alleged invoices of $660,999 paid to Anita Perrottet’s company, Macquarie Consulting, over two and a half years were her husband, Charles Perrottet’s, share of the money from Nassif.

Anita Perrottet has told the watchdog payments were for “strategic and marketing advice” she provided; while Charles Perrottet has said they were “holistic” payments covering his advice to Nassif on his developments as well as his wife’s work.

Greenwood has previously told the commission Anita’s advice, for which the commission has no written evidence, provided a “mum’s perspective”. He said after first being contracted by Beckington in 2020, she may have come up with the term “zero unnecessary euthanasia” for greyhounds, and given advice about discouraging minors from vaping, including removing flavours such as bubble gum, as well as black market regulation.

On Wednesday, Dwyer took Greenwood to 2017 recommendations by the NSW greyhound industry reform panel, which included the phrase “zero unnecessary euthanasia”, suggesting to Greenwood he had “outsmarted [him]self by coming up with that false evidence when it’s clearly a term used in a document years earlier”.

“I disagree,” Greenwood replied. Dwyer showed Greenwood a submission by Philip Morris to a 2020 Senate inquiry which referenced measures to regulate the illicit tobacco trade and a 2019 report committing to applying guidelines to prevent youth access to vapes.

Greenwood said he had read the submission by Philip Morris, a client of his, but rejected Dwyer’s suggestion it “makes a mockery” of his evidence about Anita Perrottet’s advice.

After Dwyer asked him how old Anita Perrottet’s children were at the time she provided advice on vaping, Greenwood said he did not know, and did not think it was relevant.

The presiding commissioner, Fabian Gleeson, intervened to tell Greenwood he was “not here to debate with counsel assisting” but to “answer the question”. Greenwood said: “I presume they’re under 10.”

Dwyer, telling Greenwood that Anita Perrottet’s children were around two and three at the time, asked: “Did she give you a mum’s perspective on deterring under-fives from vaping?

“No,” Greenwood replied.

Dwyer said: “Your evidence is ridiculous, can I suggest to you, that Anita Perrottet contributed to a debate that had been the subject of professional reports … for many years before you say you brought Anita Perrottet on board.” Greenwood disagreed.

Gleeson made a non-publication order over a racist message Greenwood had sent in 2020 about the chief of staff of then treasurer Dominic Perrottet.

Ellis had shared a screenshot of messages with Greenwood in which he had written to ask to be connected with a Treasury staff member on behalf of Toplace, to which the chief of staff responded: “We have no interest in doing favours for developers. All proposals will go through proper planning processes and be assessed on its merits.”

Gleeson paused proceedings, making a direction that it was in the public interest that a “racist remark” Greenwood sent to Ellis about the chief of staff be suppressed. Greenwood accepted Dwyer’s suggestion that the comment was “highly offensive”.

Ellis moved to the UK at the start of this year and is not expected to appear. Dominic Perrottet is not named as a person of interest in Icac’s allegations and is not accused of any wrongdoing.

On Wednesday afternoon, Greenwood was asked about folders shared by Anita Perrottet with him via email in March 2023 following parliamentary inquiry which preceded Icac’s probe, titled “Greyhounds”, “British Tobacco” and “Catholic Cemeteries”.

Anita Perrottet previously told the commission she ceased to work for JPG Advisory before the parliamentary inquiry. After Dwyer alleged that the empty folders which were created as a “false documents trail” – which Anita Perrottet has denied – Greenwood said he could not speculate.

Dwyer later asked: “There is no reason that you can think of to send you empty folders at any time, is there?”

“No, unless you thought in future there might be a need to fill them,” said Greenwood.

Greenwood was not released from his summons at the end of his evidence on Wednesday but is not currently scheduled to appear again before the commission. As Dwyer’s questioning of Greenwood concluded on Wednesday, she put it to him that he had put Anita Perrottet in “a very difficult position … because you and others, but let’s stick with you, were party to her lying to this [commission]”. Greenwood disagreed.

Icac’s inquiry continues.

australia.title: Minns says Molly Ticehurst’s murderer deserved longer sentence for ‘vicious’ crime’ – as it happened
australia.snippet: This blog is now closed Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast Sports precinct funding report reveals a ‘pattern of...
australia.content:
Minns says Ticehurst’s murderer should have more jail time

The New South Wales premier, Chris Minns, says Daniel Billings is a “bastard” and his prison sentence is inadequate.

Billings, 31, will spend at least 20 years behind bars, before becoming eligible for parole, for murdering his ex-girlfriend Molly Ticehurst, who was a childcare educator and young mother from Forbes, in central western NSW.

Justice Natalie Adams sentenced Billings to a maximum term of 28 years in the NSW supreme court on Friday, finding he acted out of revenge after Ticehurst reported allegations of sexual assault to police.

At a press conference earlier today, the premier was asked whether he thought Billings’ sentence was adequate. Minns responded:

No, it’s a vicious, horrible crime. I would have loved to see him far, far longer.

And obviously, we’ve changed the law since that horrific murder to have a standard non-parole period of 25 years, but you know the judge made the decision, and I just feel terrible for the family who are decent, honest, hard-working people who’ve lost their daughter at the hands of a complete bastard.

Billings was out on bail when he smashed through Ticehurst’s bedroom window and stabbed her 15 times with a hunting knife just before midnight on 21 April 2024.
