    Lambie pleads with voters to reject ‘dangerous’ and ‘delusional’ Hanson

What we learned today, Wednesday 16 September

That’s where we’ll leave the blog for today. Here were today’s top stories:

  • It was a sitting day in federal parliament in Canberra, where AI, copyright and immigration dominated the debate ahead of a speech by the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, tomorrow, which is expected to unveil Labor’s new migration policy.

  • Barnaby Joyce backed his leader, Pauline Hanson, saying she got a “10 out of 10” for issuing a lukewarm, qualified apology over her comments about Indigenous Australians and to Anthony Albanese.

  • Betting company Dabble was fined more than $1m for sending more than 800 messages to 165 gamblers who had joined the federal government’s self-exclusion register and asked to be left alone.

  • The Queensland premier announced that Anthropic, the AI giant behind the large language model Claude, has done a deal to lease the site of its first Australian datacentre in western Queensland.

  • One Nation’s New South Wales leader Mike Newman tried to clarify comments he made at a rally on Tuesday night that he wanted abortions to “stop”, saying that he “made a mistake” and the party’s policy on abortion “is clear”.

  • The Victorian premier made another policy backflip, announcing a re-elected Labor government would give police and protective services officers the power to stop and search people for knives using handheld metal detectors.

  • Cotality released its “pain and gain” report, showing one in five Melbourne apartments, and more than one in 10 Sydney units sold in the June quarter made a loss.

  • Sarah Abo announced she would finish up as co-host of Today and leave Nine at the end of the year to pursue other opportunities.

  • And veteran Network 10 journalist Hugh Riminton told his colleagues he would retire from journalism on 2 October after a 48-year career.

Minns says Ticehurst’s murderer should have more jail time

The New South Wales premier, Chris Minns, says Daniel Billings is a “bastard” and his prison sentence is inadequate.

Billings, 31, will spend at least 20 years behind bars, before becoming eligible for parole, for murdering his ex-girlfriend Molly Ticehurst, who was a childcare educator and young mother from Forbes, in central western NSW.

Justice Natalie Adams sentenced Billings to a maximum term of 28 years in the NSW supreme court on Friday, finding he acted out of revenge after Ticehurst reported allegations of sexual assault to police.

At a press conference earlier today, the premier was asked whether he thought Billings’ sentence was adequate. Minns responded:

No, it’s a vicious, horrible crime. I would have loved to see him far, far longer.

And obviously, we’ve changed the law since that horrific murder to have a standard non-parole period of 25 years, but you know the judge made the decision, and I just feel terrible for the family who are decent, honest, hard-working people who’ve lost their daughter at the hands of a complete bastard.

Billings was out on bail when he smashed through Ticehurst’s bedroom window and stabbed her 15 times with a hunting knife just before midnight on 21 April 2024.

Crackdown on reckless prescribing as regulator ramps up peptides oversight

Melissa Davey

Australia’s medical practitioner regulator is cracking down on high-volume prescribers of drugs including unapproved peptides, medicinal cannabis and GLP-1 weight-loss drugs such as Ozempic and Mounjaro.

The Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency (Ahpra) announced on Wednesday it will also soon release conflict-of-interest guidance for doctors as concerns grow about commercial influence over their prescribing.

In a statement, Ahpra said the agency has been investigating unsafe prescribing and “is concerned growing consumer demand for certain medicines, coupled with undue commercial influence, has led some practitioners to depart from established professional standards”.

The statement said:

Telehealth prescribing and the provision of certain medicines require practitioners to demonstrate even greater rigour to prevent harm to patients.

Ahpra can take regulatory action against practitioners over unsafe prescribing, with the most serious cases referred to tribunals.

Medical Board of Australia chair Dr Susan O’Dwyer warned doctors and prescribers “active in these new pharmaceutical frontiers” that they have ethical and legal obligations, saying that:

A patient may want peptides, but that doesn’t mean they need peptides. It doesn’t mean that peptides are clinically justified.

For patients, the Ahpra chief executive Justin Untersteiner, said people “should not be taking chances on black-market peptides or advice from online influencers with zero clinical knowledge or training”.

Anyone with concerns about a doctor or other health professional’s conduct should contact Ahpra.

Benita Kolovos

‘We do not want Peter’s death used to promote political agendas’: family issues statement after Victorian motorcyclist dies in reported pothole crash

The family of Peter Mason, a 71-year-old motorcyclist who died on Monday after reportedly hitting a pothole on a regional Victorian highway say his loss has “left an enormous hole” in their lives.

Mason, known as Tiki, was the president of a social motorcycle club, Eureka Social Riders, and was widely respected within the community. He died on Sunday after reportedly losing control on the Western Highway near Trawalla Road, with his death reigniting a political debate over the condition of Victoria’s roads in the lead-up to the November state election.

His family issued a statement this afternoon asking people not to use his death to “promote political agendas”. It reads:

There are no words to express the heartbreak our family is experiencing following the sudden and devastating loss of Peter Mason.

Peter was so much more than the circumstances of his death. He was a much-loved member of our family and a friend to many. His loss has left an enormous hole in our lives, and we are struggling to come to terms with a life taken far too soon.

We are aware of the public interest surrounding the circumstances of Peter’s death, including the condition of the road where the incident occurred. If, through the appropriate processes, changes are identified that could prevent another family from experiencing this devastation, we sincerely hope something positive can come from Peter’s death. However, these matters should be dealt with by the appropriate authorities.

We do not want Peter’s death used to promote political agendas, and we ask that no one speak on behalf of our family or claim to represent our views.

The family thanked everyone who had reached out with condolences, support and memories of Peter. They also asked reporters to be “respectful , factual and sensitive”.

Hugh Riminton to leave 10 and retire from journalism after near-five decade career

Veteran Network 10 journalist Hugh Riminton has told his colleagues he will retire on 2 October after a 48-year career.

Riminton made the announcement in an email to Network 10 staff earlier today, in which he said:

One of my emotions is excitement. I got my first job as a cadet reporter aged 17. I am now 65. 48 years in daily news is probably enough.

This reporter’s life has given me the world. I leave with nothing but gratitude for every hour of it.

In the coming weeks and months, I plan to support my son as he does his HSC. I also want to spend some time with my splendid Dad who is coming on 98.

Every hour is precious.

After that, I am sure projects will emerge to keep me busy.

I want to thank you all for being my colleagues and friends for the past 17 years.

There is no one among you I am not proud to work alongside.

Martin White, a vice-president of news at 10’s owner, Paramount, wrote:

As you’ve heard already, the great Hugh Riminton has made the tough decision to move on. After a near half-century on the day-to-day news, it’s an innings few of us can comprehend, let alone get close to.

While I’m sad, and will miss him greatly, I’m also proud to have been able to call him a colleague. I’ve even subbed a few of his scripts, though I can’t recall ever changing a word!

He is rightly celebrated as one of the premier journalists in this country and has had a vital impact on the Australian media, and on Australian democracy.

Sarah Abo announces she is leaving Today

Sarah Abo has announced she will finish up as co-host of Today and leave Nine at the end of the year to pursue other opportunities.

In a statement today, Abo said:

Words can’t express how grateful I am to our viewers for letting me into your homes to be part of your morning routine. Without you, there is no Today show.

Together with 60 Minutes, I’ve spent my time at Nine chasing stories, travelling and reporting from all over the world, interviewing some incredible and inspiring people from all walks of life. Becoming a mum has heralded a new chapter and sharing that with our audience has been truly special. As many of you know, this has been a significant journey for my family and will continue to be my greatest achievement.

Nine’s executive director of news and current affairs, Fiona Dear, thanked Abo and said she had been an “integral part” of the team, “bringing warmth, energy and first-class journalism to the program each morning”.

Police appeal after woman’s body found in central Queensland sand dunes

A young woman has been found dead in sand dunes days after visiting a hair salon, sparking a police appeal, AAP reports.

Payge Leembruggen, 31, was discovered by a man walking his dogs at a popular Mackay beach in central Queensland about 8am on Tuesday, police said.

She was last seen at 8.55am on Friday at an Andergrove salon, located about 6km from the beach.

Speaking to reporters in Mackay earlier today, Det Insp Emma Novosel said:

We’re trying to fill a four-day gap at this time.

That’s why we’re seeking information from members of the public.

We’re obviously going through that bushland area to try and find any items of interest that could assist us in determining what happened to Payge and how she came to be in that location.

The mother-of-one’s cause of death was unknown but an autopsy had been scheduled, Novosel said.

Leembruggen was not reported missing and it was not unusual for her to travel from her Mount Jukes address – where she lived with extended family – to Mackay, about 40km away.

Support was being provided to Leembruggen’s family who were “understandably” upset, and her young child was being cared for by family members, police said.

Leembruggen is described as Caucasian and about 178cm tall with brown hair.

She was last seen wearing a white top, bright red yoga pants and a red bow in her hair, with a small backpack-style handbag.

Police have urged anyone who saw her between Friday and Tuesday or with any information to contact them.

Benita Kolovos

First hearings announced in royal commission into Victoria’s Big Build

The royal commission into the Victorian government’s Big Build will hold its first public hearing next week.

Known formally as the “royal commission into the integrity of major public and civil infrastructure construction projects in Victoria”, the inquiry headed by Chris Kourakis confirmed it will hold its opening hearing next Wednesday.

The hearing will be held in the Melbourne magistrates court from 10am and will be live-streamed.

Catie McLeod

Hello, I hope you’ve had a nice day so far. I’ll be with you on the blog until this evening.

Krishani Dhanji

That’s all from me today folks, thanks for following along on the blog!

I’ll leave you with the brilliant Catie McLeod for the rest of the day’s news while I coax myself to go outside and get some fresh air.

See you back here tomorrow.

Tl;dr here’s what happened in question time

  • The spotlight was heavily on the prime minister and health minister Mark Butler today, who defended himself over planned cuts to private health insurance rebates for over 65s.

  • Anthony Albanese’s patience was also somewhat tested over his links to former Play School host and ex-Labor staffer Rhys Muldoon, who was yesterday stood down over “abhorrent” social media posts.

  • Tony Burke acknowledged immigration numbers do need to drop, ahead of his appearance at the National Press Club tomorrow (a month after he was first due to speak).

  • The opposition also tried to corner Labor on whether the prime minister had sought cabinet approval before extending the increase to Australia’s humanitarian intake to 20,000. Burke replied that it showed how far away the Coalition was from understanding government function.

  • And Jim Chalmers nearly got kicked out today after he called Tim Wilson a “karaoke clown”. He was referring to this.

Question time ends

After a final dixer to Kristy McBain, that was surprisingly rowdy and nearly led to housing minister Clare O’Neil getting booted, the prime minister calls time on QT.

‘All care, no responsibility’, Albanese defends private health insurance changes

Why doesn’t the government properly tax coal and gas, cut the $11bn diesel fuel rebate or reconsider the $368bn Aukus agreement if it needs to find savings, asks Monique Ryan, instead of targeting pensioners by cutting private health insurance rebates for over 65s.

It’s not a misprint – Ryan has been given a second question today, lucky her.

Anthony Albanese spends half of his answer defending Aukus, and then also defends the decision to change the private health insurance rebate.

He then takes aim at the crossbench.

I expect the Independents don’t have to come up with a budget, and that’s fine. All care – no responsibility. But as a government, we have to.

Rhys Muldoon comments ‘outrageous and completely unacceptable’ says Albanese

Before we get to the next question, Ben Small is booted, after a dixer to Tony Burke where he was railing off about the Plymouth Brethren church and their involvement in the election.

Then Tony Pasin returns to the dispatch box, and asks the prime minister point blank if he provided Rhys Muldoon a reference for his role as an Australia Day ambassador or any other role.

Anthony Albanese says it was appropriate that Muldoon was immediately stood down after several old social media posts surfaced.

There are two roles in which action has been taken. One was he was a relief staff casual employee for Senator Dowling, and the comments, when people became aware of them and the senator became aware of them, he took immediate action and that’s appropriate.

Albanese says Muldoon was an Australia Day ambassador since 2014 but was not this year.

The assistant minister has taken action today, who has responsibility for those issues, to clearly say that it is not appropriate for him to be an ambassador. I find his comments outrageous and completely unacceptable.

Butler on the defence over decision to lower private health insurance rebates for over 65s

Monique Ryan has picked up the baton and is also asking the government about its decision to lower the private health insurance rebates for over 65s. Modelling by the parliamentary budget office that she commissioned found half of the $3bn in savings would be paid for by pensioners.

She asks if pensioners were “really the only place that you could find budget savings?”

Mark Butler says, for the 50th time, that the government has had to make “hard decisions” and that it’s necessary to pay for more aged care beds and home care support.

He says the initial decision by John Howard to give over 65s a higher health insurance rebate was done in a very different economic scenario.

I would like to be able to maintain that arrangement but we have had to make some difficult decisions to find the aged care investment that is necessary.

Now in this debate there have frankly been a lot of misinformation about what the impact will be. Our modelling indicates that first of all the average impact on a private health insurance member of these changes will be in the order of 70 cents per day.

‘Zero to do with me’: Albanese distances himself from Muldoon

Anthony Albanese has tried to completely distance himself from Rhys Muldoon, the former Play School host, and brief Labor staffer who was yesterday stood down after “abhorrent” posts were unearthed.

Liberal frontbencher Tony Pasin asks what involvement Albanese had in Muldoon’s appointment as a Labor adviser and if he provided Muldoon with a reference for his Australia Day ambassador role.

Albanese says no, and no.

On the first part of that question, none. On the second part, his Australia Day role began under the former Coalition government … and his appointment had zero to do with me.

‘We do need to get net overseas migration down’, says Burke

Net migration does need to come down, says Tony Burke, ahead of his national press club address tomorrow.

Regional independent MP Helen Haines asks him whether the government will speed up visa processing for regional areas, who are struggling to get critical workers.

We do need to get net overseas migration down, we do …

To be able to work through this, we need to be able to make sure that we deal with the numbers – we need to make sure that we deal with the numbers overall and do so in a sensible, targeted way that provides the easiest pathway through for the Australian economy.

He doesn’t exactly answer the question on whether he’ll reverse the “go-slow” on visa processing for the regions.

He does say there are more tools that the government has at its disposal to improve the migration system and he’ll says he’ll have more to say about that tomorrow.

A bit of a forward sizzle, as it were.

Butler holds firm on private health insurance rebates for over 65s

Nationals MP Michelle Landry is next and asks about a warning from the Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists which says Labor’s reduction of private health cover rebates for over 65s will lead to “increased costs for older women who require gynaecological care”.

Anthony Albanese says broadly that the government has introduced the largest ever women’s health program.

The health minister, Mark Butler then takes over and says that submissions are still coming into the inquiry taking a look at the changes, and the government will consider them.

But he holds firm and maintains the changes are necessary.

We are doing this … to find necessary savings to fund more beds in aged care, more packages at home and better care, particularly changing the co-contribution arrangements which I think have been advocated by the opposition, among others, around showering and other hygiene activities.

The changes that we make restore arrangements to their original design which did not differentiate between members or private health insurance holders based on their age.

Chalmers on a warning for ‘karaoke clown’ barb

Jim Chalmers has lashed out after Tim Wilson seized on a story in Nine Newspapers reporting that the treasurer’s colleagues are worried about inflation and rate rises. Chalmers reportedly held a private briefing with backbenchers ahead of an intergenerational report.

Chalmers quips that at least he’s taken more seriously by his own colleagues than Angus Taylor is by his.

Of all the people to ask a question like this, I don’t think the karaoke clown over there …

Cue the uproar.

Dan Tehan comes to the dispatch box (stifling a laugh mind you) but Milton Dick says he’s got this one in hand, and puts Chalmers on a warning, who’s then forced to withdraw the remark.

Chalmers says:

I do take my colleagues seriously and I take our economic challenges seriously as well. It’s why I make myself available to discussions with the parliamentary party, it’s a very informed and very engaged group, and I will continue to engage with them in good faith about the most important issues.

We will take these things more seriously than those opposite take them.

Before he gets to the end, Liberal MP Henry Pike gets booted for interjecting too much.

australia.title: Foreign students to face tough restrictions on bringing in family under Labor’s immigration plan
australia.snippet: Home affairs minister Tony Burke will detail long-awaited changes as support for One Nation surges amid immigration debate Follow our Aus...
australia.content:
Foreign students will face tough restrictions on the ability to bring family members into Australia, as the federal government shifts sections of the country’s immigration system away from demand-driven settings.

Long-awaited changes will be revealed by the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, on Thursday, and are expected to include efforts to stop visa overstays and limit lengthy appeals processes for applicants.

The changes are designed to bring down net overseas migration (Nom) while doing the least damage to the economy.

Burke will address the National Press Club in Canberra, with a speech titled “The work of managing the migration program: Who arrives, who stays, who leaves”.

He had been due to announce the plans more than a month ago, but the speech was cancelled at the 11th hour amid debate inside cabinet about the direction and scale of the changes.

The plan will shift some rules for visa categories away from demand-driven settings, allowing the government more control on the numbers of people coming into, and departing, the country.

  • Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

Labor plans to use legislation to gain more control over arrival numbers, but could rely on regulation and directives to departmental officials if it cannot find agreement in parliament.

“We do need to get net overseas migration down,” Burke said.

“We need to make sure that we deal with the numbers overall, and do so in a sensible, a targeted way that provides the easiest pathway through the Australian economy.”

Labor wants policy settings tweaked to ensure it can meet forecasts for Nom, as support for One Nation surges over concerns about rates of immigration.

Last year Australia issued more than 337,000 international student visas, of which about 45,000 went to dependents or family members of the primary applicant. Under the mooted changes, the vast majority of students would be required to come alone.

As well as 185,000 permanent arrivals annually, the government wants Nom to fall from about 305,000 to about 225,000 over two years, ending years of higher than expected arrivals, including from international students and working holidaymakers.

Nom measures people coming into or leaving the country for a period of at least 12 months over 16 months, including leaving and returning Australian citizens. Nom has fallen in seven consecutive quarters since September 2023. It is forecast to fall lower than pre-Covid levels by 2027-28.

But temporary visa holder rates remain high. For the 2024-25 financial year, there were 568,370 overseas arrivals, according to Australian Bureau of Statistics data.

Changes including efforts to stop people whose visas have expired from transferring to different categories are likely, essentially forcing some overseas citizens to leave the country more quickly.

The government is also expected to seek to drive down the number of unlawful non-citizens currently in Australia.

Department of Home Affairs data shows that, as of July, there were 110,898 individuals not granted a protection visa who were yet to be deported. The total includes people on bridging visas and others seeking a judicial or administration review.

Labor’s efforts to regain the initiative on immigration comes as One Nation surges in the polls and as community sentiment on the number of overseas arrivals remains a key issue motivating voters.

One Nation said on Monday it would cut the number of temporary migrants in Australia by more than 750,000 over three years, targeting international students and family members of skilled migrants.

Business groups, universities, the aged care sector and both Labor and the Coalition all savaged the plan, warning Hanson’s proposals would hurt essential services and the economy.

Anthony Albanese tried to secure Coalition support for legislative changes in talks with the opposition leader, Angus Taylor, last week, but no agreement was reached. The prime minister leaves Australia to attend the United Nations general assembly in New York on Friday.

The independent senator David Pocock said on Wednesday the country deserved a mature conversation about immigration, not one starting with numbers.

“The big thing I would love to see is a plan. There’s this constant talk about numbers, about classes of visas. Rather than actually having the conversation as a country, what is our 10-year plan for migration,” he told ABC radio.

“What are the skills that we need? What are the trade-offs when it comes to housing, impact on the environment?”

The Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry boss, Andrew McKellar, called for an end to “the race for the lowest Nom”, warning business needed skilled workers from overseas.

“We do not have a migration problem in Australia; we have a housing crisis and skill shortages. Those are the problems we need to fix. Shortsighted approaches that damage the economy won’t solve them. Those are red lines for business,” he said.

australia.title: ‘Anywhere, anytime’: Victoria police and PSOs to get random stop and search powers after Labor backflip
australia.snippet: Premier Ben Carroll adopts Coalition’s stance on Jack’s Law, which gives police and PSOs power to randomly search people for knives with ...
australia.content:
The Victorian premier has made another policy backflip, announcing a re-elected Labor government would give police and protective services officers the power to stop and search people for knives using handheld metal detectors – despite experts warning of a lack of evidence that the measure reduces violent crime.

Ben Carroll on Wednesday announced he would match a commitment made by the Coalition opposition last year to introduce Queensland’s Jack’s Law, named after 17-year-old Jack Beasley, who was fatally stabbed in Surfers Paradise in 2019.

Under Labor’s commitment, police and PSOs would receive 1,200 extra handheld metal-detecting wands to use on any person in a public place from early next year. Or as the police minister, Paul Edbrooke, put it: “Anywhere, anytime.”

The bipartisan support for the new powers comes despite warnings from criminologists and human rights advocates that the laws will be ineffective at reducing violence.

Sarah Schwartz, the legal director of the Human Rights Law Centre, accused Carroll of “ignoring the evidence and caving into pressure in a race to the bottom to suppress democratic freedoms and human rights”.

“We know from other states that these powers only serve to give police unchecked powers to harass and target people, particularly marginalised groups, while doing nothing to actually keep communities safe,” she said.

Gemma Cafarella from Liberty Victoria said there was “no evidence that these kind of laws keep people safe”.

“Instead, the evidence shows that these powers would be disproportionately used against people of colour who are innocently going about their lives and who have not done the wrong thing,” she said, noting that police already have the power to search people where it is reasonable to believe that they have a weapon.

A Griffith University study of a 12-month trial of Jack’s Law on the Gold Coast between 2021–22 found there was no reduction in violence as a result of the searches and that they put human rights at risk.

“There’s no evidence that it’s in any way effective in actually reducing knife-related violence, which is the whole premise of the law,” Griffith University’s Janet Ransley told the Guardian last year.

Swinburne University criminologist Joel McGregor said “tough-on-crime policies” would do little to address the causes of crime, particularly among young people.

“Police might find a knife or a weapon and they remove that weapon from the street. That’s a great outcome, but it doesn’t address the underlying behaviours as to why that person is carrying the knife or the weapon in the first place,” he said.

Currently in Victoria, police are only authorised to perform warrantless pat-down searches in “designated areas”. A six-month designation of the CBD as one was earlier this year deemed invalid by the federal court.

Carroll said the government would work with legal experts to ensure Jack’s Law would be “watertight”.

“Victorians are sick of knife crime, and so am I,” he told reporters.

Jack’s Law has also been replicated in Tasmania, Western Australia and the Northern Territory following advocacy by Jack’s parents. In New South Wales, the warrantless search powers apply only in declared designated areas.

Victorian Labor’s move marks a significant shift for the state government after it had resisted expanding search powers under their former leader Jacinta Allan.

After meeting with Beasley’s parents in September 2025, the then police minister, Anthony Carbines, said the state’s search powers were sufficient.

“It might not be called Jack’s Law, but what we have in place in Victoria is a safe and effective mechanism that Victoria police asked for,” he said at the time.

Asked repeatedly why there had been a policy change, Carroll answered: “I’m the new premier.”

The Victorian Greens’ justice spokesperson Katherine Copsey said the about-face showed Labor had “completely lost its way on community safety” and was “just copying whatever the Liberals announce”.

According to Queensland police statistics, police stopped and scanned 160,997 people between 18 July 2025 and 30 June 2026. More than 77% of them were male, and 22.6% of people with a known ethnic origin were Indigenous, despite Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people making up only 4.6% of Queensland’s population.

In Victoria, two years of data obtained by Liberty Victoria revealed just over 1% of the searches conducted in designated areas found illicit items, including weapons.

But Carroll’s shift was welcomed by Jack’s father, Brett Beasley, who said it was “about bloody time”.

“I’ve been pushing for Jack’s Law to be introduced down there for some time now, so it’s great news,” he told ABC Radio Melbourne.

“Put the politics aside and let’s focus on the community safety and that’s what Jack’s Law is all about.”

Additional reporting by Andrew Messenger

australia.title: Sydney man who allegedly called 13-year-old Muslim girl a ‘terrorist’ berates judge after bail refused
australia.snippet: Omar Yassine was arrested and charged with stalking and intimidation after allegedly hurling insults at year 8 student wearing a hijab Ge...
australia.content:
A middle-aged man accused of a “disgusting” Islamophobic attack on a 13-year-old girl has berated a judge after he was denied bail

Omar Yassine made an eventful court appearance on Wednesday after being held by police overnight for allegedly verbally abusing the Muslim schoolgirl on a Sydney bus.

Yassine told the court he had “hurled a few insults” at the girl, her friends and someone he thought was a teacher on Thursday but claimed he had not been the instigator.

“I didn’t threaten or intimidate anyone,” the 50-year-old, who did not want legal representation, said from the Bankstown local court dock on Wednesday.

“All I did was raise my phone ... a person alleged I took a photo [of them].

“There were four students hurling threats and abuse at me.”

The police prosecutor said there was strong evidence against Yassine, who the court heard had a 46-page criminal record.

The evidence included a video, recorded by the 13-year-old girl on an inner-western Sydney bus, that showed Yassine calling her a barrage of names, the prosecutor said.

The year 8 student, who was wearing a hijab and her school uniform, was allegedly called a “fucking terrorist” and an “immigrant dog” among other insults in the clip, later shared online.

The girl and other passengers reported the tirade to police after getting off the bus at Strathfield station.

Officers arrested Yassine at a home in nearby Greenacre after the girl and her mother went public about the incident on Tuesday.

He was charged with stalking and intimidation with intent to cause fear.

In the video, the teen told the man she was born in Australia and reminded him of her young age, but that didn’t stop the alleged abuse.

The girl and her mother told the ABC the incident was “really disgusting”.

In court, Yassine repeatedly interrupted the police prosecutor and acting judge Gary Still.

The 50-year-old said he should be released on bail because he would be able to report to police and was not a risk of committing another serious offence.

Judge Still disagreed.

“This is a vulnerable victim, a 13-year-old on public transport,” the judge said.

“There are a number of matters on your record ... and you are just off a community corrections order.”

Upon being refused bail, Yassine turned his disdain on the judge.

“You’re pre-empting my behaviour ... how did you come up with that conclusion?” Yassine said as he was led off to the cells.

“Good work, Your Honour – bow down to them, mate.”

The abuse allegedly began after the 13-year-old stood up for another girl in a hijab who believed Yassine was taking photos of her without her knowledge.

The Strathfield state MP Jason Yat-sen Li said he was “horrified and deeply angry” about the alleged incident, while congratulating the teen for speaking up.

“Let me be absolutely clear: Strathfield will not tolerate racist or Islamophobic abuse, particularly when it targets children,” he said.

Yassine was not required to enter a plea and will return to court at a later date.

world.title: US to bar some South Africans over claims of anti-white discrimination
world.snippet: Announcement of visa restrictions follows Trump’s false claims of ‘white genocide’ taking place in South Africa The US has announced visa...
world.content:
The US has announced visa restrictions on some South Africans as Donald Trump’s administration continues to claim that South Africa’s government racially discriminates against white minority Afrikaners.

The announcement did not specify individuals who were barred from the US. Trump has spent his second term falsely claiming there is a “white genocide” in South Africa and railing against its affirmative action policies.

Since the start of last year, the US has cut aid to South Africa, barred it from this year’s G20 summit in Miami and set up a refugee programme for Afrikaners and other South African racial minorities. Meanwhile, the Trump administration has been dismantling refugee and asylum programmes for people fleeing war and persecution.

“The South African people are being failed by a government that is destroying its economy through an obsessive pursuit of racial grievance against the Afrikaner minority,” the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said in a post on X.

“The South African government has consistently failed to adequately address rural crime, violent and dehumanising rhetoric, and race-based discriminatory policies against Afrikaners and other minority populations.”

The US visa restrictions would target “foreign nationals who enact or enable policies that promote race-based discrimination, incite violence, or enable land confiscation without compensation in South Africa”, Rubio added.

The US ambassador to South Africa, the conservative media activist Leo Brent Bozell III, said on X: “As has been made absolutely clear, the time for endless ‘dialogue’ has run its course … This visa restriction policy is only the first step in a series of escalatory measures that will show America’s firm resolve in this matter.”

South Africa’s foreign ministry said in response that its policies were being misrepresented. “The announcement, once again, aligns with the mischaracterisation of South Africa’s domestic policies by fringe groups who wrongly portray themselves as representatives of “minorities” and Afrikaners in general,” ministry spokesperson Chrispin Phiri said in a statement that was first published in Afrikaans.

Phiri added: “It is our sovereign right to put in place laws that address the nation’s concern over centuries of racial injustice … South Africa respects that the United States may hold different views regarding particular measures and their implementation.”

Afrikaners, who are descended from Dutch and French settlers, ruled South Africa during apartheid. The regime discriminated against and repressed the country’s black majority, while keeping white people safe and wealthy.

Since Nelson Mandela took office as South Africa’s first black president in 1994, South African governments have tried to redress the country’s racial inequality, including through Black economic empowerment policies and buying land to redistribute.

These efforts have had limited impact. White South Africans typically have 20 times the wealth of Black people, according to a 2023 article in the Review of Political Economy, an economic journal.

Nonetheless, some white South Africans claim they are now the victims of racial discrimination, allegations that US conservatives have long promoted.

Rubio’s visa restrictions announcement criticised land expropriation without compensation. South Africa introduced a law last year that allows the government to seize land without paying for it in specific circumstances, including if it is abandoned or only held for speculation. There is no large-scale expropriation of land.

Among white South Africans who think they are discriminated against, many cite the far-left opposition leader Julius Malema’s repeated use of apartheid-era chant “Kill the Boer”, Boer being another word for Afrikaner. A video featuring the chant was played by Trump when he met South Africa’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa, in the Oval Office last year.

The ruling African National Congress party has disavowed the chant, which South African courts have ruled is not meant literally and therefore not hate speech.

world.title: ‘We are prey’: discovery of seven women’s bodies fuels anger over femicide in South Africa
world.snippet: String of female murder victims found near Johannesburg’s international airport, including five in the past week The discovery of the bod...
world.content:
The discovery of the bodies of seven women around Johannesburg’s international airport, including five in the past week, has prompted an outpouring of fear, grief and anger over a lack of progress in tackling femicide.

When Elizabeth “Tsontso” Moselakgomo did not return after going for a run on 9 September, her eight-year-old daughter alerted relatives, who contacted police. The 38-year-old’s body was found on Saturday and identified by relatives on Monday. The news of her disappearance had gone viral.

Police said in a statement on Saturday that four women’s bodies had been found since 15 July in Kempton Park, across the highway from OR Tambo international airport. All were half-naked and with visible bruising.

On Monday and Tuesday, two more bodies were found in Olifantsfontein, about 15 miles north of Kempton Park. On Tuesday, police said another woman’s body had been found 25 miles to the south-east, naked and decomposed.

“In this country we are prey,” Sakane Mokoena posted on Instagram after confirmation of the death of her friend and fellow runner Moselakgomo.

South Africa has one of the highest rates of femicide in the world. In the year to 31 March 2024, more than 27,600 people were murdered, 5,578 of them women, according to the latest police data.

For years, women have called on the South African government to take gender-based violence seriously. After hundreds of women protested on the eve of the G20 summit in Johannesburg in November 2025, President Cyril Ramaphosa declared it a national crisis.

However, the lack of a concrete plan or action has frustrated campaigners – and women keep being killed.

The latest deaths are being investigated by specialist officers, who said on Saturday: “Women in and around Kempton Park are urged not to walk or run alone, particularly in isolated areas. They should avoid secluded spaces, remain vigilant and, where possible, travel or exercise in groups.”

South African women responded with anger at the idea that they had to be responsible for their own safety, with many runners noting they already took precautions, such as sharing routes. “We are tired of being told to be vigilant when women are already doing everything possible to stay alive,” said the advocacy group Women For Change.

“It should not take a missing woman, a desperate family, runners and communities searching, and a case going viral, before an area is searched with this intensity,” the group said.

Detectives said on Saturday that they were examining a serial killer angle. However, on Monday, a police spokesperson, Athlenda Mathe, told reporters: “For now, nothing tells us that we’ve got a serial killer.”

Mathe added that a suspect in the killing in July of the first woman, her boyfriend, was in custody.

Ramaphosa said on Tuesday that he had directed police authorities to prioritise the ongoing murder investigations.

Although the gender of the suspect or suspects in the other killings has not been confirmed, campaigners called on men to take responsibility for violence against women and children.

“When some of these things happen in our presence, most of us men tend to look the other way,” said Bafana Khumalo, a co-executive director of Sonke Gender Justice.

“You have excuses like ‘No, it’s not my business’. We feel strongly that violence against women is our business. We need, as men, to begin to face each other squarely and hold each other accountable.”

The identification of Moselakgomo’s body has triggered an outpouring of grief.

Mokoena met her about two years ago, when Moselakgomo joined a running club so she did not have to train alone on Saturdays.

“She’s an amazing woman,” said Mokoena. “She always spoke about her daughter. Tsontso always said ‘Bye guys, I have to go, I have to go to my child’.

“That’s just an example of how close she was with her baby girl. And she was a really light-spirited, funny and joyful woman, who was kind – very, very kind.”

Running clubs around South Africa organised events to remember Moselakgomo and Mokoena said she hoped this would help push the government and police to do more to protect women.

She added: “I’m just happy that the world, or at least our country, was standing still for a moment to acknowledge what is happening. Let’s get this out there and figure out exactly what is happening to women.”

world.title: Al-Qaida and IS-linked violence in Africa’s Sahel belt set to hit record levels this year
world.snippet: Twenty-five years after 9/11, figures compiled by conflict monitor underline how Sahel region has become centre of Islamist terror Islami...
world.content:
Islamist extremist violence in Africa’s Sahel region is set to reach historic highs after a series of sweeping offensives by groups linked to al-Qaida and Islamic State, according to new figures compiled by the conflict monitor Acled.

As the US marks the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks launched by al-Qaida against targets in Washington and New York, the statistics underline the continued expansion of the veteran organisation in parts of Africa – in stark contrast with its relative weakness elsewhere.

Compiled by Acled, which stands for Armed Conflict Location and Event Data, the statistics focus on the centre of Islamic militancy in three countries – Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger – which together comprise a huge and hotly contested zone at the heart of the strategic Sahel region.

According to the respected non-profit organisation, incidents of violence with jihadist groups present in the three countries have soared from 63 in 2016 to 2,845 in 2025. So far this year, 2,145 events have already been logged. If current trends continue in coming months, an annual total of well over 3,000 events appears likely.

Though total deaths from terrorism globally have fallen to their lowest level since 2008, those in the Sahel have risen sharply.

“Terrorism has become more geographically concentrated: the Sahel continued to record some of the world’s highest terrorism death tolls, with the UN recording more than 9,000 deaths from security incidents across Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger in 2025,” the 2026 report of the Global Peace Index noted earlier this year.

In April, a joint offensive in Mali launched by the al-Qaida-linked group Jama’at Nusrat ul-Islam wa al-Muslimin (JNIM) and the Tuareg-dominated rebel group Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) targeted strategic towns, government forces and their Russian auxiliaries with ambushes, car bombs, drones and raids, inflicting significant casualties.

Mali’s defence minister died in a suicide attack on his residence in the garrison town of Kati, 9 miles north-west of the capital, Bamako, and the head of military intelligence was killed.

Other attacks hit Mali’s international airport, while rebels seized control of the strategic city of Kidal, a former stronghold of the FLA, after soldiers fled and a force of Russian mercenaries surrendered. The defeat reversed a key symbolic victory won by the junta in Mali three years ago.

Since then, JNIM has continued to expand areas under its control in Mali, killing more soldiers and Russian mercenaries in recent weeks, and broadening its operations in some neighbouring countries.

Much of the violence involves fighting with rival groups. The conflict has also included multiple killings by government armed forces and Russian mercenaries.

In Burkina Faso, JNIM has claimed more than 130 attacks in 2026, striking closer to Ouagadougou, the capital. In Niger, the group claimed at least 17 attacks but remained significantly less active than its rival Islamic State in the Greater Sahara, according to a recent United Nations report based on intelligence supplied by member states.

Experts said JNIM had distanced itself from al-Qaida’s historic objectives of striking the US and its allies.

“In the Sahel, Islamic State and al-Qaida now command big areas but these are very localised groups. Not a single attack in Europe or the US has been planned in the Sahel,” said Ulf Laessing, a senior analyst at the Konrad Adenauer foundation in Berlin.

The other main group in sub-Saharan Africa with links to al-Qaida is al-Shabaab, which has dominated much of Somalia’s rural areas for many years.

“In east Africa, al-Shabaab remains one of the continent’s deadliest groups, with Acled recording more than 10,000 reported deaths in al-Shabaab-related violence over the past 18 months,” said Peter Bofin, Acled’s senior analyst for south-east Africa. “Despite some degradation of its extortion in Mogadishu, its revenue streams stretch across the country, and the region.”

Militant groups linked loosely to IS are active in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Mozambique, Chad and Nigeria, where they were targeted by US airstrikes last year.

The continuing expansion in sub-Saharan Africa has been welcomed in al-Qaida’s propaganda, but experts point out the continent barely featured in the group’s strategic planning until recent years. “Twenty-five years ago it was all about Afghanistan and then Iraq … Africa wasn’t really of interest then. Now its the main area of operations,” said Laessing.

Though sectarian and ethnic conflict, bitter competition over resources, poor governance, endemic instability and other factors make Africa a fertile ground for Islamic militant recruiters, territory in places like Mali and Somalia has major limitations as a base for campaigns elsewhere in the world or for long-range terrorist attacks.

At its peak in the years after the 9/11 attacks, al-Qaida affiliates posed a significant threat to authorities across much of the Middle East, with thousands convinced by the group’s call for a global uprising against the US, Israel and local regimes. Al-Qaida was also able to inspire and direct a series of lethal attacks in Europe that killed hundreds.

However, the recent UN report described al-Qaida senior leadership as “marginalised” and noted that the group’s capability and intent to conduct external operations remained “unclear”.

Analysts point out there has been no formal declaration of a successor to Ayman al-Zawahiri, the veteran Egyptian militant killed in Kabul by the US in 2022.

Instead, the de facto leader is believed to be 66-year-old Saif al-Adel, who is thought to have been in Iran since 2002 and has yet to make any public statement. Other leaders are likely to be based in Afghanistan, where the group has been able to rebuild a limited infrastructure, western intelligence services believe.

The most potent al-Qaida affiliate outside Africa is the Yemen-based Al-Qaida in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP), which the UN report described as “the vanguard of the global al-Qaida movement” and one of the few affiliates committed to continuing al-Qaida’s decades-old campaign against the US.

In May, AQAP’s media channels released a new video calling on Muslims in Europe and the US to carry out local attacks and to fight on “behalf of the [Islamic community] in any way possible”.

But though AQAP continues to maintain an estimated 2,000 fighters, largely entrenched in the mountains between Abyan and Shabwa, the group’s activity fell by approximately 70%, from 63 events in the first seven months of 2025 to 19 during the same period in 2026, according to Acled.

Some analysts have contrasted the high numbers of militants currently mobilised by groups such as JNIM and al-Shabaab, which number in the tens of thousands, with the much more limited manpower available to al-Qaida before the 9/11 attacks. Others stress the very different intentions and capabilities of the group now and 25 years ago.

world.title: Slave-trade wealth was embedded in Britain’s financial system, research finds
world.snippet: Dozens of Bank of England directors and founding subscribers invested in trafficking of enslaved Africans The Bank of England and the Bri...
world.content:
The Bank of England and the British financial system were for centuries deeply involved in the enslavement and transatlantic trafficking of millions of African people, according to new research on Britain’s slavery history.

Research by historians compiling the Register of British Slave Traders has found that the scale of the financial system’s involvement in enslavement is greater than previously known or acknowledged. The Bank of England, the central bank owned by the government since nationalisation by Clement Attlee’s Labour administration in 1946, had dozens of financiers involved in its foundation who were also significant investors in the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans.

Dr Michael Bennett of the University of Sheffield, who has conducted extensive research on the Bank’s historical involvement in enslavement, has found that 24 directors were investors in the trafficking of enslaved African people. Four were among the London elites who were founding directors of the Bank in 1694. The other 20 were in office at Threadneedle Street over the next century.

The last, Christopher Puller, was a shipper of weapons for the slave trade and co-owner of a 1786 voyage that trafficked enslaved people from the Gambia to Jamaica, according to the register. Puller was a director for 11 years before he died in 1789. Nine of the 24 were also governors of the Bank.

Bennett also researched the founding subscribers to the Bank of England, finding that at least 30 invested in the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans. At their head were the king and queen of the day, William III and Mary II, who held shares in the Royal African Company. It is clear, Bennett said, that wealth generated from the slave trade formed part of the Bank’s initial capital.

“Slave traders and their wealth were firmly embedded within Britain’s, especially London’s, private banks and financial corporations during the 17th and 18th centuries. They shaped the development of the financial system,” he said. “Banks and other institutions, like insurers, provided the financial services that supported, and made great wealth from, the transatlantic slave economy.

“The Bank of England supported this system throughout, and directly provided financial services to the slave trade. Its clients included the Royal African Company and the South Sea Company.”

An archetypal example of a Bank of England director in the register is John Rudge, the MP for Evesham. He was a director of the Bank between 1699 and 1740, and governor in 1713-15. Rudge was also a shareholder and assistant (director) in the RAC and deputy governor of the South Sea Company.

The findings of the register add to the research carried out by historians behind the Legacies of British Slavery (LBS) archive at University College London, which documents owners of enslaved people on plantations. That research found that 16 past governors of the Bank of England and 26 directors had a financial interest in the ownership of enslaved people and plantations in the period before abolition in 1833. The Bank itself, and the Treasury, were centrally involved in paying out £20m, the equivalent of £23bn today according to one method of calculation, in “compensation” to enslavers under the abolition legislation. Nothing was paid to the people who had been enslaved and trafficked.

The Black Lives Matter protests of 2020 prompted several high street banks and financial institutions to acknowledge their historical involvement in slavery. Dr Nicholas Draper, who led the LBS research, was also a lead investigator for the register and he discovered many more historic slave traders who were founders of private banks and other financial organisations.

Research by Bennett after the BLM protests found that the Bank of England had owned 599 enslaved people on two plantations.

An exhibition at the Bank in 2022 included the names of the enslaved people. Most of the men, women and children listed had European names such as Pierre, Catherine and Alexandre, with no information about the country from which they were taken.

The Bank also acknowledged and apologised for past governors and directors having been involved in the slave trade.

Humphry Morice, a longtime director and governor from 1727-29, was also an MP and defrauded the Bank to fund his trafficking operations.

Morice was described by Prof Matthew David Mitchell, in an article published on the Bank’s website, as “the biggest London-based trafficker of enslaved human beings from Africa to the British colonies in America.” Morice was responsible for equipping about 110 ship voyages between 1704 and 1732, transporting more than 30,000 enslaved men women and children to Jamaica, Barbados, Virginia and elsewhere in America, Mitchell wrote. “This was his principal commercial activity, and it is for this that he must chiefly be remembered.”

While the Bank has acknowledged this history and apologised, the Treasury has not publicly done so. This is in line with the government’s position of resisting the discussion of reparations and not acknowledging culpability for the centuries of trafficking and enslaving.

Bennett’s further findings will increase the pressure on the government to do so, which is building from Caribbean and African countries.

A Bank of England spokesperson said it had explored its connections to enslavement in depth in its 2022 exhibition, adding: “We are grateful for Dr Bennett’s collaboration on that work.”

In 2023, the Scott Trust, the Guardian’s sole owner, published research showing that the founder of the Manchester Guardian and his backers profited from the enslavement of African people in Jamaica and the US. In response, the Scott Trust launched the Cotton Capital series and the Legacies of Enslavement programme, a 10-year restorative justice initiative.

world.title: ‘I believed the hype’: the white South Africans denied refugee status in the US
world.snippet: Drive to save thousands of Afrikaners from false claims of ‘white genocide’ appears to show signs of slowing When Donald Trump announced ...
world.content:
When Donald Trump announced in February 2025 that the US would accept Afrikaners from South Africa as refugees, many white South Africans who believed that they were victims of racism in their country thought that their prayers had been answered.

However, in the past few months, dozens of applicants to the refugee programme have been rejected, with many left dismayed and confused as to why they would be left to face what Trump has falsely claimed is a “white genocide” in South Africa.

After Trump’s February 2025 executive order announcing the resettlement programme, which was expanded to include members of a “racial minority”, the first group of 68 white South Africans arrived in the US that May. The US also shut down the refugee programme for anyone else fleeing war and persecution.

Since then, more than 13,000 have moved to the US, according to state department figures. Arrivals are also accelerating, with more than 2,600 admitted in August.

Afrikaners, descended from Dutch and French settlers, ruled South Africa during apartheid. The regime repressed the black majority, while keeping white people safe and wealthy.

Since the end of apartheid more than 30 years ago, affirmative action policies have helped to create a black elite and middle class. But about 38% of black South Africans are unemployed, compared with 9% of white South Africans, according to official data.

Meanwhile, the “black economic empowerment” policies, along with high crime rates that affect everyone, have fostered a feeling among some white South Africans that they are now the victims of racial discrimination.

The racist far right has also long highlighted brutal murders of white South African farmers, claiming them as evidence of white people being targeted. Official crime data does not show farmers or white people experiencing crime at higher rates. That has not stopped Trump amplifying these claims, in the face of the South African government’s furious rebuttals.

On 30 June, Facebook and WhatsApp groups for prospective and successful refugee applicants began to light up with news that people had begun to receive rejection letters.

“We are writing to inform you that, following review, USCIS [US Citizenship and Immigration Services] found your application to be ineligible for continued processing for resettlement to the United States at this time. This cannot be appealed,” the letters said, according to multiple rejections seen by the Guardian.

It is unclear how many have been found ineligible. USCIS did not provide data on the total number of refugee applications and rejections. One WhatsApp group set up to support rejects, called Hope beyond the Letter, had 311 members as of 10 September, according to one of the administrators, who noted that the membership fluctuated.

While the ineligibility letters did not give reasons for rejection, some applicants were given more information after making Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests. The WhatsApp group administrator, a 64-year-old freelance TV professional, who did not want his identity disclosed, found that his case was initially “recommended for approval”. However, the recommendation was reversed because his ex-girlfriend, whom he had applied with, had a marijuana conviction.

“I cried like a baby,” he said, of receiving the rejection letter on 30 June, having finished the screening process in November. “It was something I actually believed was attainable. I believed the hype.”

Pieter and Liesl (not their real names) were told they were “conditionally approved” as refugees last November. Both are Afrikaners who had a grandparent killed on a farm and were managing a farm when they applied to become refugees.

Pieter said he was convicted of trespassing in 2014, for which he said he paid a fine and did not go to court. He was granted multiple temporary visas to work on farms in the US between 2011 and 2024.

The couple’s youngest daughter was born in the US and is a US citizen. In the response to their FoI request, they noticed that USCIS had recorded her nationality as South African and incorrectly said that she would be left behind if they moved to the US as refugees.

They had already sold their house, car and many of their possessions when they received a rejection letter on 24 July. “We have to start all over again,” Pieter said.

Another applicant blamed not being able to speak in his native Afrikaans for what he claimed were misunderstandings that led to him and his wife being rejected. The reasons given in response to their FoI request were “crime involving moral turpitude” and “commission of acts of torture or extra judicial killing”.

The 67-year-old had admitted to shooting at least one black person when working as a security guard in 1995, but said it was in self-defence while responding to the mass break-in of an alcohol shop. “I was thoroughly investigated by the authorities,” he said. “I was not charged, because I did not break the law.”

In an emailed response that did not address specific cases, the USCIS spokesperson Zach Kahler said: “The Department of Homeland Security is committed to resettling Afrikaner refugees who are being persecuted by the South African government.

“[USCIS] reviews each refugee application on a case-by-case basis … [and] notifies aliens found ineligible for continued processing through the US Refugee Admissions Program, including those found ineligible for public safety concerns or criminal histories. This cannot be appealed. This administration will always prioritize the safety and welfare of the American people.”
